title: A boy leaves the east
hook: Jalal al-Din is born around 1207 in the eastern Persian world, and his family walks west as the Mongols approach

segments.voice: Yesterday, two books for one camp: a Persian poet and a Roman emperor, side by side. Your line was two voices. Which one are you more curious about? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

Think of the last time you packed up a whole life. Boxes, a truck, the house you grew up in shrinking in the mirror. Now picture it around the year 1216, in the far east of the Persian-speaking world, near what is now northern Afghanistan. A respected preacher gathers his family, his books and his students, and starts walking west. His little son is about nine. The boy's name is Jalal al-Din Muhammad. He will not come back. Years later, when he's famous, people will call him by the name of the place where he ended up. Today, the boy who left the east.
screen: `PACKING UP A WHOLE LIFE.` → `AROUND 1216, WALKING WEST.` → `A BOY LEAVES THE EAST.`

segments.voice: Start with the birth. Tradition says Jalal al-Din was born in 1207 in Balkh, an old city of scholars. Some modern historians think it was really Vakhsh, a smaller town in today's Tajikistan, where his father was working at the time. Either way, he was born in the eastern Persian world, and Persian was his language. His father, Baha al-Din Walad, was a preacher and a teacher of religion, a serious man who wrote down his own inner life in a notebook the family kept. Then the leaving. Somewhere between 1216 and 1220 the family set out. The old accounts say they went ahead of the Mongols, whose armies swept through the region and wrecked Balkh around 1220. Some scholars add that Baha al-Din had quarrels at home too. We don't know every reason, and the sources don't agree. What we know is the road: Baghdad, a pilgrimage to Mecca, then years in towns across Anatolia, the land that is now Turkey. On the way the boy grew up, married young, and lost his mother. Around 1228 the family settled in Konya. And here's the thing to tell a friend tonight. Anatolia had once been part of the Roman Empire, so people in the east called it Rum, Rome. A man from Rum was Rumi. The poet the whole world knows is named after where he landed, not where he started. In Iran and Afghanistan many call him Mowlana, our master, instead. Keep that road in mind all camp. A lot of his poetry is about being far from where you began.
screen: `BORN 1207, EASTERN PERSIAN WORLD.` · `THE FAMILY WALKS WEST.` · `BAGHDAD, MECCA, ANATOLIA, KONYA.` · `RUMI MEANS FROM RUM, ROME.` · then, large: `THE ROAD WEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a place you left. A town, a house, a school, a country, a friendship. Settle and let it come. What did it smell like? What did the light do in the afternoon? Who was there? Don't judge whether leaving was right. Just let yourself stand there again for a minute. Then notice who you became because you left. The bell holds the time.
A boy leaves the east. Jalal al-Din, born around 1207, walking west with his family to Konya, and named Rumi for the land where he arrived. Today's word.
screen: `A BOY LEAVES THE EAST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the road west. Today, when you pass something that reminds you of a place you left, say your line and notice what you carried with you. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Visitors from many countries travel to Konya, in Turkey, to the museum and tomb of Rumi, and his birthplace is honored in Afghanistan and Tajikistan as well; readers often start with the story of his family's long journey west.

fork.setup: you're Baha al-Din, around 1216. armies are coming from the east, and you have a family and a household of books. what do you do?
options: stay and hope the storm passes.
take the family and walk west.
send the boy alone to safety.
fork.reveal: the family walks west together, through Baghdad and Mecca to Anatolia. Balkh was wrecked around 1220; the boy grew up on the road.

original.note: Persian: from Rum, the old Roman land of Anatolia. a name for where he landed.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rumi was a poet's name, like a pen name.
what it means: Jalal al-Din Muhammad, born around 1207 in the east, called Rumi after the land he settled in.
what a scholar hears: Balkh by tradition, Vakhsh by some modern historians; Rum was Anatolia, once Byzantine, the Eastern Roman Empire.

sources.work: Franklin D. Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West (2000) (paraphrased)

sources.ref: Account of Baha al-Din Walad's departure

notes: Birth year 1207 and birthplace: Balkh is the traditional account; Franklin Lewis argues for Vakhsh (today's Tajikistan). Both named without deciding. Confirm.
Departure date given as 'between 1216 and 1220'; motives (Mongols, and possible local quarrels) hedged. Confirm the hedge.

Route summarized as Baghdad, Mecca pilgrimage, Anatolian towns (Malatya, Erzincan, Larende/Karaman), settling in Konya around 1228. Confirm; the script says he married young and lost his mother on the way (Larende).
Baha al-Din's 'notebook' is the Ma'arif; described loosely. Confirm.
Name: 'Rumi' from Rum (Anatolia, former Byzantine/Roman territory); 'Mowlana' used in Iran and Afghanistan. Confirm spelling Mowlana vs Mawlana.
Balkh destroyed by the Mongols around 1220/1221. Confirm.
